USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Finish the Section 301 record and put a structured IP/tech-transfer negotiation on the table before firing China-wide tariffs. Keep the January Section 201 safeguards in place, do not roll them back, and do not convert the February 16 Section 232 steel/aluminum menu into a global tariff blast that hits allies. Offer Beijing a defined path off the coming 301 remedy list in exchange for enforceable changes on forced transfer, JV/equity limits, discriminatory licensing, and cyber-enabled theft—not another package of commercial MOUs.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is mildly negative (slight U.S. opportunity) because the dispute is still in the U.S. initiative phase and is not yet imposing a GDP or export shock. The August 14, 2017 memorandum and subsequent 301 initiation framed a real long-term problem—forced tech transfer, non-market licensing, directed acquisition of U.S. technology, and cyber theft tied to industrial plans such as Made in China 2025—but as of March 1 the investigation is still open (statutory clock runs a full year from August 18, 2017) and no 301 tariffs or entity-list action have been imposed. The November 8, 2017 Beijing visit produced a large commercial-deal package that yielded no substantive concessions on those structural issues, which is why the current state is an opportunity to apply unused leverage rather than a crisis already damaging the U.S. economy. Macros confirm the dispute is not biting: February consumer sentiment is 99.7, industrial production is still rising, the yuan has strengthened (DEXCHUS 6.328 on Feb 28), and Chinese reserves remain ~$3.15 trillion. The goods trade gap is politically salient—BOPGTB widened to −$74.6 billion in February and the 2017 China goods deficit was reported at a record $375 billion—but that is a grievance and a source of leverage, not a recessionary shock. Action should stay near hold/negotiate because (1) firing 301 remedies before findings are issued would jump the legal process and hand Beijing a WTO/unilateralism talking point it has already previewed (MOFCOM “strong dissatisfaction,” Gao Feng warning of “all necessary measures”); (2) China’s reaction to the January 22 Section 201 solar/washer tariffs has so far been protest and a WTO posture, not a farm-belt retaliation cycle, so there is nothing to “retaliate” against and no case for concession; and (3) Commerce’s February 16 Section 232 options (24% global steel or 53% on a 12-country list including China; 7.7% global aluminum or 23.5% on China and others) are the higher-risk tool—allies and U.S. downstream users (autos, Business Roundtable) have already signaled retaliation and cost shocks, which would spend alliance capital the United States needs if 301 later requires a coalition. The disciplined move is therefore to negotiate under the shadow of a nearly complete 301 case, not to escalate tariffs now and not to give away 201 relief for another empty MOU.
key_factors: Section 301 investigation open (initiated Aug 2017; findings not issued; 12-month clock)
Nov 2017 Beijing summit: commercial MOUs, no structural IP/tech-transfer concessions
Section 201 solar/washer safeguards already in force; China protested, no material retaliation yet
Section 232 steel/aluminum recommendations public (Feb 16) but presidential decision not due until April; global options hit allies
U.S. real economy healthy (sentiment, IP); bilateral goods deficit large and widening, China FX/reserves stable
Beijing rejected 301 consultations and previewed countermeasures if the U.S. acts unilaterally

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump signs memorandum directing USTR to investigate China's IP and technology-transfer practices under Section 301. USTR investigation initiated.
Trump visits Beijing; large package of commercial deals announced (many MOUs). No substantive concessions on structural IP / tech-transfer issues.
Trump approves Section 201 safeguard tariffs on solar panels and washing machines (China among suppliers hit). First major tariff action of the administration.
University of Michigan consumer sentiment 99.7 as of 2018-02-01; no collapse in household confidence.
U.S. industrial production 101.7085 (2017=100) in February 2018, still rising over the window.
U.S. goods trade deficit widened to -$74,571 million in February 2018 from -$66,665 million in October 2017.
CNY/USD 6.328 on 2018-02-28, yuan stronger versus ~6.53 in early September 2017; no China FX-stress signal.
China reserves ex-gold about $3.15 trillion in February 2018, essentially stable.
USTR initiated 301 on Aug 18, 2017 on forced transfer, discriminatory licensing, directed acquisition of U.S. tech, and cyber-enabled IP theft; determination due within 12 months.
February 1, 2018 USPTO brief: 301 still an open investigation; China IP/tech/innovation policies are the core; one year to conclude.
Jan 2018: Trump/Cohn said a 301 'fine'/remedy was coming soon; businesses cite hundreds of billions in lost technology from forced transfer and theft.
2017 U.S. goods deficit with China rose to a record $375 billion; 301 described as a separate probe that could restrict Chinese imports over forced technology transfer.
China called Section 201 an 'abuse of trade remedy measures' and 'overreaction' and said it would work with other WTO members; no tariff counterstrike reported.
Feb 16, 2018: Commerce recommended 24% global steel tariff or 53% on 12 countries including China, and 7.7% global aluminum or 23.5% on China/HK/Russia/Venezuela/Vietnam; Trump deadlines in April.
Allies braced for 232; Business Roundtable warned of foreign retaliation; automakers warned higher metal costs would hit U.S. competitiveness.
MOFCOM: U.S. use of domestic law for 301 is 'irresponsible' and 'not objective'; expressed strong disapproval of the investigation.
Jan 20, 2018: draft 301 report circulating; China views 301 as unilateral aggression; Gao Feng warned China would 'take all necessary measures' if the U.S. insisted on unilateral protectionism.
